ingestion.notes: Read the full v1 preprint. Exact accuracy numbers are only shown in figures, which weren't readable from the PDF text, so results are described qualitatively.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: An LLM proposes the top 3 candidate cell types from a cluster's marker genes, then CZ CELLxGENE expression data picks the final label, which beats both LLM-only (GPTCelltype) and database-only annotation and reduces hallucination.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: LLMs like GPT-4 annotate clusters well from marker genes but can hallucinate, and nothing grounds their answer in real expression data.

sections.heading: Method: two stages
sections.body: Stage 1: an LLM is prompted with the tissue and marker genes and returns its three most likely cell types, in order. Stage 2: for each candidate, the agent looks up how strongly and how widely the marker genes are expressed in that cell type in CZ CELLxGENE Discover (for the given species and tissue, or across tissues if the tissue is unknown). A selection score adds the LLM's rank to the expression-based ranks, and the highest-scoring candidate wins.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.body: Nine datasets (303 cell types from 36 tissues), reusing the GPTCelltype benchmark: Human and Mouse Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, HuBMAP Azimuth, GTEx, CNS B-cell lymphoma, colorectal and lung cancer. Scored with GPTCelltype's Cell Ontology agreement score, and compared with GPTCelltype, CELLxGENE alone and PanglaoDB.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: CellTypeAgent beat every comparison method on all nine datasets. Stronger base models (best: o1-preview) gave better results, and the gain over LLM-only annotation was largest with weaker models. With the open-source DeepSeek-R1 it improved by 5.1%, which matters where data privacy rules out closed models. CELLxGENE alone often couldn't separate similar types (e.g. pericytes vs. mural cells); the LLM step narrows the choices first.

sections.heading: What didn't help
sections.body: Adding literature snippets (LitSense) or NCBI gene summaries to the prompt made results worse: the LLM over-relied on the pasted text, prompts got costlier, and many papers report markers only in figures or supplements.

key_findings: Verification against a real expression database reduces hallucination and improves accuracy
Using the top 3 LLM candidates worked slightly better than other candidate counts
More marker genes generally improved annotation
Can flag mixed populations when told a sample might be a mixture
limitations: Short preprint (not peer-reviewed in this version); figure-level numbers not given in text
Depends on the cell types and tissues present in CELLxGENE
Takes marker gene lists as input; clustering and marker selection happen upstream
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred) and Dr. Talkington's own 'useful' example. It's the closest design to our project: an agent that combines LLM reasoning with database verification. The finding that pasting literature into prompts hurts accuracy is directly relevant to how our agent should use the ingested papers.

preprocessing.summary: Takes the marker gene lists from the GPTCelltype benchmark; marker selection is upstream of the method.

clustering.summary: Assumes clusters already exist; annotates one cluster's marker list at a time.

annotation.summary: Two-stage agent: LLM proposes ranked top-3 candidates, then CELLxGENE scaled expression and expressed-fraction of the markers re-rank them; the top-scoring candidate is the label. Optional literature and gene-summary tools were tested and rejected.

algorithms.name: CellTypeAgent selection score
algorithms.description: LLM candidate rank + rank of summed marker expression + rank of expressed fraction + cross-tissue expression rank.

algorithms.name: CELLxGENE-only lookup
algorithms.description: Pick the cell type with the highest average marker expression, without an LLM.
